L2@P0: Homomorphisms on noncommutative symmetric
L3@P0: functions and permutation enumeration

L5@P0: 1Department of Mathematics, Brandeis University
L6@P0: 2Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Davidson College
L7@P0: Abstract. We present a unifying framework for deriving permutation enumeration
L8@P0: formulas involving restrictions on descent compositions or permutation statistics
L9@P0: describable in terms of descent compositions: these formulas can be proven by first
L10@P0: lifting them to the algebra of noncommutative symmetric functions and then applying
L11@P0: an appropriate homomorphism. We give several applications of this method including
L12@P0: rederivations and extensions of classical results in the literature as well as new results.
L13@P0: Keywords: permutation statistics, noncommutative symmetric functions, descents,
L14@P0: inversions, peaks, shuffle-compatibility
L15@P0: 1 Introduction
L16@P0: Let π = π1π2 · · · πn be a permutation in Sn, the set of permutations of [n] = {1, 2, . . . , n}.
L17@P0: Let |π| be the length of π, so that |π| = n whenever π ∈ Sn. We say that i ∈ [n − 1] is a
L18@P0: descent of π ∈ Sn if πi > πi+1.
L19@P0: Every permutation can be uniquely decomposed into a sequence of maximal increasing
L20@P0: consecutive subsequences—or equivalently, maximal consecutive subsequences containing
L21@P0: no descents—which we call increasing runs. For example, the descents of π = 85712643 are
L22@P0: 1, 3, 6, and 7, and the increasing runs of π are 8, 57, 126, 4, and 3. The composition of n
L23@P0: whose parts correspond to the increasing run lengths of π is called the descent composition
L24@P0: of π and is denoted Comp(π). Thus, Comp(π) = (1, 2, 3, 1, 1) for π = 85712643.
L25@P0: There are many classical results in the literature that count permutations with various
L26@P0: restrictions on descent compositions. For example, David and Barton [4] showed that

L47@P1: In a series of recent papers [11, 21, 22, 10], the present authors show that permutation
L48@P1: enumeration formulas involving restrictions on descent compositions (or involving
L49@P1: permutation statistics that can be described in terms of the descent composition) can
L50@P1: be proven under a unifying framework by deriving a lifting of the formula in the
L51@P1: algebra Sym of noncommutative symmetric functions and then applying an appropriate
L52@P1: homomorphism. We use this very general method to prove a myriad of new formulas
L53@P1: as well as to provide a new derivation of David and Barton’s formula (1.1) and of other
L54@P1: formulas previously obtained by Carlitz [1], Chebikin [3], Elizalde [5], Elizalde–Noy [6],
L55@P1: Petersen [14, 15], Remmel [17], Stanley [18, 19], and Stembridge [20].
L56@P1: The purpose of this extended abstract is to outline this method of permutation
L57@P1: enumeration, summarize some of the work done in the papers [11, 21, 22, 10], and to
L58@P1: describe new developments in this domain which utilize the theory of shuffle-compatible
L59@P1: permutation statistics. We begin in Section 2 by introducing preliminary definitions and
L60@P1: ideas from permutation enumeration and the basic theory of noncommutative symmetric
L61@P1: functions, including a key reciprocity formula from the first author’s Ph.D. dissertation
L62@P1: [8] which is used to obtain many noncommutative symmetric function formulas necessary
L63@P1: for our applications. In Section 3, we define three homomorphisms on noncommutative
L64@P1: symmetric functions and demonstrate several applications of our method using these
L65@P1: homomorphisms, including a rederivation of (1.1). Finally, in Section 4, we explain how
L66@P1: each “shuffle-compatible descent statistic” induces a new homomorphism that can be
L67@P1: used to count permutations by the corresponding “inverse statistic”, and present a few
L68@P1: applications of these homomorphisms for the descent and peak number statistics.

L470@P7: Recently, the present authors initiated the study of shuffle-compatible permutation
L471@P7: statistics [12]. Roughly speaking, a permutation statistic st is said to be shuffle-compatible

L478@P7: A permutation statistic is called a descent statistic if it depends only on the descent
L479@P7: composition. For example, the descent number, alternating descent number, major index,
L480@P7: comajor index, and peak number are all descent statistics, but the inversion number inv is
L481@P7: not. Given a descent statistic st, we write st(L) to mean the value of st on any permutation
L482@P7: with descent composition L. Thus every descent statistic st induces an equivalence relation
L483@P7: on the set of compositions in the following way: we say that compositions J and K are
L484@P7: st-equivalent if |J| = |K| and st(J) = st(K). For example, the compositions J = (3, 1, 4)
L485@P7: and K = (2, 4, 2) are des-equivalent.
L486@P7-8: The following is one of our main theorems in [12], relating the study of shufflecompatible descent statistics to the theory of quasisymmetric functions.9

L488@P8: homomorphism φst : QSym → Ast, where Ast is a Q-algebra with basis {aα} indexed by
L489@P8: st-equivalence classes α of compositions, such that φst(FL) = aα whenever L ∈ α.
L490@P8: Here, we note that Ast is called the shuffle algebra of st and the multiplication of its
L491@P8: basis elements aα encode the distribution of st over shuffles of permutations.
